extracted.intended_audience: graduate students / advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry; readers of Ravi Vakil's 'The Rising Sea'.
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, computational criteria, and pathologies for scheme-theoretic images and closures; definitions and algebraic criteria for locally principal subschemes, effective Cartier divisors, regular sequences, regular embeddings, and complete intersections. Intended as textbook guidance and exercises for working with these notions in scheme theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme-theoretic image (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If i: Z ↪ Y is a closed subscheme with ideal sheaf I_{Z/Y}, the image of π: X → Y lies in Z if the composition I_{Z/Y} → O_Y → π_* O_X is zero. The scheme-theoretic image of π is the intersection of all closed subschemes of Y containing the (set-theoretic) image; equivalently, the smallest closed subscheme containing the image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informally: locally, functions vanishing on the scheme-theoretic image are precisely those that pull back to 0 on X. In the affine case the scheme-theoretic image is cut out by elements of B that pull back to zero in Γ(π^{-1}(Spec B), O_X). Alternate names: 'closed subscheme-theoretic image', 'image closed subscheme'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local computation via I(B) (definition and method)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Y = Spec B is affine, define I(B) := ker(B → Γ(π^{-1}(Spec B), O_X)). Then the scheme-theoretic image on Spec B is cut out by I(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To glue these affine descriptions one must check compatibility with localization: for g ∈ B there is a map φ_g: I(B)_g → I(B_g) and injectivity is clear; surjectivity is the issue (see next item). Use this to compute scheme-theoretic image afﬁne-locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local surjectivity criterion (practical condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surjectivity of φ_g amounts to: given r/g^n on D(g) that pulls back to zero on π^{-1}(D(g)), there exists m such that r g^m pulls back to zero on π^{-1}(Spec B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful sufficient conditions include: (i) π^{-1}(Spec B) reduced (then take m=1, using that a function on a reduced scheme is zero if zero at every point); (ii) π^{-1}(Spec B) affine (then r' = 0 on D(g') implies some m with r'(g')^m = 0); (ii)' more generally if π^{-1}(Spec B) is quasicompact, cover by finitely many affines and take m = max(m_i). Quasicompactness is repeatedly useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 9.4.4 (when scheme-theoretic image computed afﬁne-locally)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a morphism of schemes and X is reduced or π is quasicompact, then the scheme-theoretic image of π may be computed afﬁne-locally: on Y = Spec A it is cut out by the functions in A that pull back to 0 on π^{-1}(Spec A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies computing the image by the kernel ideal I(B) on affines under these hypotheses. See Corollary 9.4.5 for a consequence about underlying sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 9.4.5 (underlying set = closure of set-theoretic image)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 9.4.4 (X reduced or π quasicompact), the closure of the set-theoretic image of π is the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image is closed and contains the set-theoretic image, so contains its closure; on the complement of that closure π^{-1} is empty, hence scheme-theoretic image is empty there under the hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: When set-theoretic image equals underlying set (finite/projective case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the set-theoretic image is closed (for example, if π is finite or projective), then the set-theoretic image is the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a useful special case arising frequently in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathologies / counterexamples for scheme-theoretic image
rubrics_metrics.description: In pathological situations the underlying set of the scheme-theoretic image need not be the set-theoretic image; it is only guaranteed to be closed and to contain the closure of the set-theoretic image under hypotheses. Example 4: X = Spec k[ε^n]/((ε^n)_n) mapping to Y = Spec k[x] by sending ε_n to x on the nth component leads to scheme-theoretic image = Y while set-theoretic image = {0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that nonreduced/fuzzy source schemes can produce unexpected global behavior; the examples illustrate 'fuzz' collapsing or persisting under maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheme-theoretic closure of a locally closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: The scheme-theoretic closure of a locally closed embedding π: X ↪ Y is defined to be the scheme-theoretic image of π (also called the schematic closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an intrinsic closed subscheme of Y that is the 'smallest closed subscheme containing X' and is useful for interpreting locally closed embeddings in several equivalent ways under suitable hypotheses (see Exercise 9.4.C and Corollary 9.4.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced reduced subscheme structure on a closed subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a closed subset X_set ⊂ Y there is a canonical reduced closed subscheme X (the induced reduced subscheme) whose defining ideal on Spec B is the radical ideal I(X_set ∩ Spec B), so X corresponds to Spec B/I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, construct W as disjoint union of residue fields of points of X_set and take the scheme-theoretic image of the canonical map ρ: W → Y; X is the smallest closed subscheme whose underlying set contains X_set. Exercises ask to check X is reduced and its underlying set is X_set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of a scheme (Y_red)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reduction Y_red of a scheme Y is the closed subscheme obtained by quotienting affine coordinate rings by their nilradicals: on Spec B it is Spec(B / N(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the 'reduced version' of Y obtained by 'shearing off the fuzz'. Caution 9.4.11: globally Γ(U, O_Y) modulo nilpotents need not equal Γ(U, O_{Y_red}) in all cases (functions can be locally nilpotent without being nilpotent globally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally principal closed subscheme (definition and remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme X ↪ Y is locally principal if there is an open cover {U_i} of Y such that for each i, X ∩ U_i = V(s_i) for some s_i ∈ Γ(U_i, O_Y) (i.e., the ideal sheaf is locally generated by a single element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hypersurfaces in P^n_k. Warnings: 'principality' is not affine-local; a locally principal closed subscheme need not be cut out by a global function. The phrase 'locally principal' is used in different contexts elsewhere in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Cartier divisor (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme X ↪ Y is an effective Cartier divisor if the ideal sheaf is locally generated by a single non-zerodivisor: there exists an affine cover Spec A_i of Y with X|_{Spec A_i} = V(t_i) scheme-theoretically where t_i ∈ A_i are non-zerodivisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: the ideal sheaf is locally principal and generated by a non-zerodivisor at each point. This is central; 'locally principal' itself is less central. Note: being an effective Cartier divisor can be verified on a suitable affine cover but not on an arbitrary affine cover (not an obviously affine-local condition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of effective Cartier divisor via associated points (exercise 9.5.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a locally Noetherian scheme X, a global function t ∈ Γ(X, O_X) defines V(t) which is an effective Cartier divisor iff t doesn't vanish at any associated point of X. More generally, a locally principal closed subscheme is an effective Cartier divisor iff it doesn't contain any associated point of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a practical test in Noetherian situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular sequence (definition 9.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an A-module M, a sequence x_1,...,x_r ∈ A is an M-regular sequence if (i) for each i, x_i is not a zerodivisor on M/(x_1,...,x_{i-1})M (with i=1 interpreted as x_1 not a zerodivisor on M), and (ii) (x_1,...,x_r)M ≠ M (proper inclusion). For M=A this is an A-regular sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: geometrically, successive effective Cartier divisors imposed locally. Exercises note localization preserves condition (i); variations include replacing x by powers x^N under controlled circumstances (Exercise 9.5.E). Regular sequences are an algebraic approximation to 'complete intersection'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-dependence and Noetherian-local remedy (Theorem 9.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity of a sequence can depend on the order in general (example 9.5.5). However, if (A,m) is Noetherian local and M a finitely generated A-module, then any M-regular sequence in m remains regular upon any reordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows global (non-local) pathologies; the theorem uses Noetherian local hypotheses. Exercises guide a proof: first the r=2 case using a spectral-sequence-style double complex, then swap adjacent elements inductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular embedding (definition 9.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A locally closed embedding π: X ↪ Y is a regular embedding of codimension r at p ∈ X if in the local ring O_{Y,p} the ideal of X is generated by a regular sequence of length r. It is a regular embedding of codimension r if this holds at all points of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can be thought of as a local complete intersection notion; exercises show the condition is open (if true at p then true in a neighborhood). Relation: effective Cartier divisor ↔ regular embedding of codimension 1 under Noetherian-like hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of the regular embedding condition (exercise 9.5.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a locally closed embedding π: X ↪ Y of locally Noetherian schemes is a regular embedding at p, then there exists an open neighborhood of p in X where π is a regular embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to affine case: if ideals agree after localization at p, they agree in some neighborhood. Use finiteness (Noetherian) and the module K = J/I trick to propagate vanishing from p to some localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Cartier divisor ↔ regular embedding of codimension 1 (exercise 9.5.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed embedding X ↪ Y of locally Noetherian schemes is a regular embedding of codimension 1 iff X is an effective Cartier divisor on Y (Noetherian hypotheses can be relaxed to coherence of O_Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: effective Cartier divisor always implies regular embedding of codimension 1; the converse needs Noetherian-like hypotheses (counterexamples exist without them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Codimension r complete intersection (definition 9.5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A codimension r complete intersection in a scheme Y is a closed subscheme X that can be written as the scheme-theoretic intersection of r effective Cartier divisors D_1,...,D_r such that at every p ∈ X the equations corresponding to D_i form a regular sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'complete intersection' means 'codimension r complete intersection for some r'. This mixes both global scheme-theoretic intersection condition and local regular sequence condition at every point.
